S1Result: Playwright's healer agent fixed every broken test. Ten repairs in under five minutes. None of them wrong.
One release later the healed CSS suite failed all seven tests again.
Healing put the suite back exactly as fragile as it was. Here is why.
S2Setup: The testbed is a small task manager app in three versions. The behaviour never changes. Only the markup does.
Version two is a redesign. Every ID and class is renamed. Two buttons become icon buttons. One test ID is renamed.
Version three is a CSS modules migration. Every class is hashed. Accessible names and test IDs stay the same.
Seven scenarios are written three ways. CSS selectors. Role locators. And test IDs.
S3Drift: Against the redesign the role locator suite passed five of seven. Test IDs passed six.
Every test logs in first. Three login selectors took out all seven tests.
S4Heal: Then Playwright's test healer agent took the ten failures. It repaired all ten in four minutes and thirty six seconds. Every repair was correct.
Every repair was in kind. A CSS selector came back as a new CSS selector.
An accessible name came back as a new accessible name. A test ID came back as a new test ID.
S5NextRelease: Then the healed suites ran against version three.
Role locators and test IDs passed seven of seven. The healed CSS suite passed none.
The username selector had been renamed again. The repair from the last round now pointed at nothing.
A second round took three minutes and twenty three seconds. It repaired all seven again. This time to hashed class names.
The healer's own report warned that these names were likely to change on the next rebuild. It repaired them in kind anyway.
S6Count: Count the repairs across two releases.
The CSS suite needed fourteen. Role locators needed two. Test IDs needed one.
Locator strategy decided the maintenance cost. The healer only paid it again each release.
S7Signal: Two of those role locator failures were real changes for users. Done became Complete. Add became Add task.
A screen reader user hears that change. The healer repaired both tests and nobody decided if the change was wanted.
So use the healer to propose fixes in a pull request. Keep a person deciding why each test broke.
One caveat. I wrote the drift myself. The app is small and I tested one healer. Run it on your own suite before you trust the numbers.
S8EndCard: Every suite and every number is in the public repo. The links are in the description.
